E'Feng was another temple cat brought back by a Daoist. 
He was named for his teeth—sharp as a blade. 
Maybe too sharp... The Daoists once debated whether E'Feng was truly a cat, or one of the mythical beasts from ancient texts. 
He once spent time in the Hanlin Academy. Didn't read many classics, but sure heard his fill of gossip and tales. 
These Daoists aren't nearly as knowledgeable as the scholars. 
And by the way, he poops just fine. No need to worry about "things that go in but never come out."

... It has been five years since I accompanied the princess to her marriage, so far from home.

The snow falls so heavily tonight. She called for me again, to bring Yuenu's Wine of Longing.

The princess is never one for drink, but perhaps tonight the moon reminds her too much of the one that shines over Chang'an. She drank cup after cup, her weeping inconsolable.

I saw it with my own eyes—crimson tears of blood fell from her lashes, though she seemed not to feel them. One drop landed on the hairpin in her hand, just before she flung it far into the dark lake.

She clutched my hand, her whispers of the Tang tongue too faint to be understood.

I know she is homesick. But what can I do...?
Is her fate not my own?

7976403689854888533:
To Lord Zhang,

Amid the turmoil within the Uhu, long has it been since I last wrote. Though I maneuver within the wolf's den, I have failed to broker peace between the Tang and the Uhu—a matter of profound regret.

I recall our wager of yesteryear: whoever first stabilized Liangzhou and united Hexi would be the victor. Today, I am a captive, my life hanging by a thread; yet your banners have not reached Liangzhou, so you too have not yet won.

I am now unarmed, with naught but this command hairpin. Within it are hidden the records of my years in this land; upon its surface, my title is engraved as a prayer for a peaceful era. I gift this pin to you. When that prosperous age arrives, and the historians set down their brushes, you must remind them to write of my title.

The world is in chaos; I fear I shall not see the day you win our wager. When the willows are green once more, pluck a branch and cast it into the river. Let it be a message, a boast to me that you have finally won.
